title: 2 Chronicles 33:1–9
context: The Chronicler retells Manasseh’s reign from 2 Kings 21:1–9: he rebuilds the high places, fills the temple with altars and an idol, sacrifices his children in the valley of the son of Hinnom, practices sorcery, and leads Judah into evil worse than the nations. Small differences in wording from Kings are noted rather than harmonized.

verses.text: Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Manasseh begins to reign at twelve and reigns fifty-five years. Arminian readers see, as in the 2 Kings 21 account, a long reign whose length makes the king’s chosen path all the more consequential for Judah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the regnal summary framing what follows. The Chronicler omits the name of Manasseh’s mother given in 2 Kings 21:1, one of several small differences between the two accounts that are noted rather than harmonized.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, after the abominations of the nations whom the LORD cast out before the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Manasseh “did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, after the abominations of the nations.” Arminian readers see a king who knowingly led Judah into the practices God had judged in Canaan.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the same verdict given in 2 Kings 21:2. The comparison with the nations prepares for the Chronicler’s account of judgment and, distinctively, of later restoration.

verses.text: For he built again the high places which Hezekiah his father had broken down; and he raised up altars for the Baals, made Asheroth, and worshiped all the army of the sky, and served them.
verses.arminianNotes: He rebuilds the high places Hezekiah had broken down, raises altars for the Baals, makes Asheroth, and worships the army of the sky. Arminian readers see a deliberate undoing of his father’s reforms.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Manasseh reversing Hezekiah’s faithfulness. The plural “Baals” and “Asheroth” differ slightly from the wording in 2 Kings 21:3, and the Chronicler does not mention Ahab here.

verses.text: He built altars in the LORD’s house, of which the LORD said, “My name shall be in Jerusalem forever.”
verses.arminianNotes: He builds altars in the LORD’s house, of which the LORD said, “My name shall be in Jerusalem forever.” Arminian readers see sacrilege in the very place God chose for his name.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the temple defiled. The Chronicler’s wording of God’s promise includes “forever,” heightening the contrast between God’s purpose and Manasseh’s altars.

verses.text: He built altars for all the army of the sky in the two courts of the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: He builds altars for the army of the sky in both courts of the LORD’s house. Arminian readers see idolatry filling the sanctuary, leaving no space reserved for the worship of the LORD alone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the thoroughness of Manasseh’s apostasy, as in 2 Kings 21:5. Star worship in the temple courts shows how deeply false worship had penetrated Judah’s life.

verses.text: He also made his children to pass through the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom. He practiced sorcery, divination, and witchcraft, and dealt with those who had familiar spirits and with wizards. He did much evil in the LORD’s sight, to provoke him to anger.
verses.arminianNotes: Manasseh “made his children to pass through the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom.” Arminian readers name this plainly as child sacrifice, forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10, and grieve the children lost to idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise grieve this grave evil, done “to provoke him to anger.” The Chronicler speaks of “children” and names the valley, where 2 Kings 21:6 speaks of “his son”; the account remains sober, without detail.

verses.text: He set the engraved image of the idol, which he had made, in God’s house, of which God said to David and to Solomon his son, “In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will put my name forever.
verses.arminianNotes: He sets the engraved idol in God’s house, of which God said, “In this house, and in Jerusalem … I will put my name forever.” Arminian readers see an idol placed where God’s name was meant to dwell.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the image set against God’s promise to David and Solomon. Where 2 Kings 21:7 names the Asherah image, the Chronicler speaks of “the idol,” a difference noted rather than resolved.

verses.text: I will not any more remove the foot of Israel from off the land which I have appointed for your fathers, if only they will observe to do all that I have commanded them, even all the law, the statutes, and the ordinances given by Moses.”
verses.arminianNotes: God had said, “I will not any more remove the foot of Israel from off the land … if only they will observe to do all that I have commanded them.” Arminian readers see the conditional nature of dwelling in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the condition attached to the promise. Readers in this tradition hold that God’s covenant faithfulness is not undone by the condition, while Judah’s disobedience brings real consequences.

verses.text: Manasseh seduced Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that they did more evil than did the nations whom the LORD destroyed before the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: “Manasseh seduced Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that they did more evil than did the nations.” Arminian readers see both king and people responsible for their rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the king leading the people astray. The Chronicler does not include the innocent blood of 2 Kings 21:16 or the prophetic oracle of 21:10–15, moving instead toward Manasseh’s exile and repentance.
